skill.name: component-refactoring
skill.description: Guides refactoring of high-complexity React components in the Dify frontend using hook extraction, component splitting, and complexity analysis.
skill.summary: Refactor complex Dify React components into smaller, testable pieces.
skill.author: langgenius

security_audit.summary: No prompt injection, credential exposure, data exfiltration, or system reconnaissance intent was found in the reviewed skill files. Most static findings are Markdown, TypeScript examples, or file path references; the remaining confirmed findings are legitimate local pnpm command instructions that require user confirmation.

remediation.issue: The skill instructs agents to run local pnpm scripts.
remediation.suggestion: Require explicit user approval before running each pnpm command, and show the exact command and working directory first.

remediation.issue: Command examples accept a component path placeholder.
remediation.suggestion: Validate that user-supplied paths stay inside the intended Dify web directory before running analysis commands.

content.value_statement: Large React components are hard to test and maintain when state, effects, and UI are mixed. This skill guides Claude, Codex, or Claude Code through Dify-specific hook extraction, component splitting, and complexity checks.
actual_capabilities: Identifies when a React component exceeds Dify complexity and line count thresholds.
Suggests custom hook extraction for state, effects, API calls, forms, and modals.
Plans component splitting around UI sections, conditionals, modals, and list items.
Applies Dify frontend conventions for services, workflow nodes, configuration, and tools.
Recommends verification with local complexity analysis, linting, type checks, and tests.
limitations: It is tailored to the Dify frontend structure and may not fit unrelated React projects.
It provides guidance and examples, but it does not include executable refactoring scripts.
It depends on local project commands being present in the target repository.
It does not replace manual review of behavior after each refactoring step.

use_cases.title: Prepare a Complex Component for Testing
use_cases.description: Reduce state, effect, and rendering complexity before adding frontend tests.

use_cases.title: Review Refactoring Scope
use_cases.description: Estimate which parts of a Dify component should become hooks or sub-components.

use_cases.title: Stabilize Feature Changes
use_cases.description: Break a risky UI change into smaller steps that can be checked after each extraction.

prompt_templates.title: Review One Component
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner review of a single complex component.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the component-refactoring skill to review this Dify React component. Identify the main complexity drivers and suggest the first safe extraction step.

prompt_templates.title: Extract State Logic
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate hook extraction for state and effects.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the component-refactoring skill to plan a custom hook extraction for this component. Focus on related state, effects, API calls, and return values.

prompt_templates.title: Split UI Sections
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced component splitting for a large UI surface.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the component-refactoring skill to split this Dify component into focused sub-components. Preserve existing props, callbacks, and directory conventions.

prompt_templates.title: Create a Refactoring Plan
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced staged refactoring across several concerns.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the component-refactoring skill to create an incremental refactoring plan. Include extraction order, verification steps, and risks to check after each step.

output_examples.input: A Dify app configuration component mixes model state, dataset selection, modal state, and publishing actions.
output_examples.output: The assistant recommends extracting model configuration and modal state first, then splitting header, content, and modal sections.

output_examples.input: A workflow node panel has many nested conditions and repeated action handlers.
output_examples.output: The assistant suggests lookup tables, early returns, a node interaction hook, and separate panel UI components.

output_examples.input: A component remains complex after one extraction and needs another pass.
output_examples.output: The assistant compares remaining complexity drivers and proposes the next smallest refactoring step with verification commands.

best_practices: Run local checks after each extraction before changing another concern.
Keep extracted hooks focused on one state or data domain.
Follow existing Dify directory and service hook conventions.
anti_patterns: Do not split a small, readable component only to satisfy a pattern.
Do not create many tiny hooks that hide simple local state.
Do not change behavior and refactor structure in the same step without checks.

faq.question: When should I use this skill?
faq.answer: Use it when a Dify React component is large, complex, or difficult to test safely.

faq.question: Does it only work for Dify?
faq.answer: The examples and conventions target Dify, but the refactoring ideas can inform similar React projects.

faq.question: Can it change code automatically?
faq.answer: The skill provides guidance for an AI assistant. Any edits still need review and verification.

faq.question: What checks should I run after refactoring?
faq.answer: Use the project complexity analyzer, linting, type checks, tests, and manual behavior checks.

faq.question: Does it handle API logic?
faq.answer: Yes. It recommends moving component-level API calls into React Query or Dify service hooks.

faq.question: What is the main risk?
faq.answer: Over-refactoring can make simple code harder to follow, so each extraction should solve a visible problem.
